finding.claim: Mass assignment: PUT /me copies the entire request body onto the authenticated user object and persists it, so any user can modify fields they should not control (e.g. role, isAdmin, id, email-verified flags, tenant/org id), leading to privilege escalation or account/identity tampering.
finding.source: req.body (JSON) of PUT /me, controlled by any authenticated user
finding.sink: Object.assign(req.user, req.body) followed by req.store.save(req.user) persisting arbitrary attributes

trace.note: Object.assign merges untrusted req.body into req.user with no field allowlist
req.store.save persists the modified user, including attacker-set privileged fields

finding.guards_checked: No allowlist, schema validation, or role/field filtering in this file. The router has no local auth middleware; req.user is assumed to be set upstream (not in this codebase, so unverifiable). The sibling route at line 11 shows the intended allowlist (displayName, bio), which this route lacks. Object.assign uses own enumerable properties, so JSON-parsed __proto__ keys are defined as own properties and do not pollute the prototype via assign, but arbitrary privileged fields are still writable.

verdict.reason: users.js:5 does Object.assign(req.user, req.body) with no allowlist or validation, users.js:6 persists it, and the sibling route at users.js:11-12 shows the intended allowlist; the only file in the codebase is users.js, so any upstream auth sets req.user for low-privilege users and nothing blocks writing fields like role.
